rationales.quote: I think it would be the opposite problem.
rationales.explanation: Jake suggests adoption may face resistance rather than simply inconsistent use across teams.

rationales.quote: The coaches won't want the kids to have the mouth guards
rationales.explanation: He believes coaches may resist the product because it would create responsibility to remove players from games.

rationales.quote: It's the parents, not the schools, who would buy these mouth guards, right?
rationales.explanation: Jake asks who the actual purchaser is, probing the proposed customer and sales channel.

rationales.quote: if it's just one kid, especially if you light up
rationales.explanation: He points to the social stigma of an individual child visibly triggering the product as an adoption barrier.

rationales.quote: So these are all just conversations you've got going on with these folks?
rationales.explanation: Jake probes whether the reported opportunities are merely discussions rather than committed traction.

rationales.quote: Breaking is a concern though.
rationales.explanation: He identifies product breakage as a concern about the solution's operational reliability.

rationales.quote: right now it's just a non-functional model
rationales.explanation: The non-working prototype limits confidence in the product's current feasibility and supports his refusal.

rationales.quote: I don't think you'll be able to get piecemeal adoption, because I think the kids are going to rebel against it.
rationales.explanation: Jake expects user resistance to prevent gradual adoption, creating a go-to-market barrier.

rationales.quote: I don't think you can build a really great business on just these hardware sales.
rationales.explanation: He views the current hardware-only monetization model as insufficient for a large long-term business.
